newsitem.title: USA: K.C. Fed's Hoenig backs broad banking reform.
newsitem.headline: K.C. Fed's Hoenig backs broad banking reform.

text.p: Thomas Hoenig, president of the Federal Reserve Bank of Kansas City, Wednesday said he backs broad banking regulatory reform as technology and non-bank competition alters the way Americans invest their money.

But any regulatory changes need to protect the system used to process payments made through banks and other financial institutions to maintain confidence in the payment system, Hoenig told a banking conference held by the Kansas City Fed.

"We need to modernize our banking and regulatory system," Hoenig said. "But there has certainly been no consensus in the legislature on this matter as well, and, as a result, comprehensive banking reform has stalled."

Hoenig declined comment on unemployment, wage pressure and other economic matters, citing a Fed policy of not commenting on matters related to monetary policy in the week preceding a meeting of the Federal Open Market Committee. The FOMC will gather on Nov. 13.

The Kansas City Fed chief said it is too early to tell whether Congress and the Clinton administration in its final term will attempt to tackle comprehensive banking reform, but increased competition from non-banks and emerging technologies like online banking will force the issue.
For decades, efforts have failed to tear down the Glass-Steagall Act, a Depression-era law that separates commercial and investment banking.
However, the administration on Wednesday signaled it was willing to make another push for broad banking regulation reform.
U.S. Treasury Undersecretary John Hawke earlier told Reuters that a plan from the department to merge the thrift and bank industry charters will also include proposals on broadening power for banks.
Also, there have been some signs of a softening of the stance held by sectors of the insurance industry that had vehemently opposed granting banks greater access to their business.

Hoenig said any proposed regulatory structure should allow banks to fail, but at the same time put in place a system of collateral or other assurances to protect the system of transferring payments to and from banks.
By protecting the payment system, regulators could ensure an isolated bank failure would not trigger a crisis in the banking system, he said.
